questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.4 Compilation against interpretation on a stated cost model, where the one-off compilation cost is the whole of the decision and the per-run comparison points the wrong way
questions.challenge_mechanism: The per-run comparison is six to one in favour of the compiled form and the one-off cost is large enough to reverse that verdict for the first forty-seven executions. A candidate who compares the running times -- which is what the phrase "which is faster" invites -- reaches the wrong recommendation with correct arithmetic at every step. The question also separates the three analysis stages, which students routinely compress into "the compiler finds the errors".

stimulus.title: A configuration language for a mail-order catalogue
stimulus.body: A retailer maintains a small configuration language, `catcfg`, used to describe how a printed catalogue's pages are built from a product database. A script is about $12\,000$ tokens long, is stored as a text file, and is run once each weekday morning to generate that day's catalogue layout. When a price band changes, an editor edits the script by hand and the next morning's run uses the edited version. The engineering team is deciding between two ways of running it: an interpreter that reads the script and executes it directly on every run, and a compiler that translates the whole script into an intermediate form which is then executed. Measured on the retailer's server, the interpreter consumes $1.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token on each run, and the compiler consumes $60\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token once when it translates the script and $0.25\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token on each run of the translated form. For this question you may ignore the cost of starting either program and the cost of reading the file from disk.

questions.question: The engineering team has asked for a recommendation on how to run `catcfg`, grounded in the costs given in the stimulus. Identify which stage of translation detects each of the three faulty fragments, explain one advantage the compiled form has for this particular workflow, determine when the two approaches cost the same across a sequence of runs, and comment on whether that figure should decide the choice.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three faulty fragments of a `catcfg` script are given below. For each one, identify the stage of translation that detects it -- lexical analysis, syntax analysis or semantic analysis -- and justify your choice.
(i) `price + 1@5`  (ii) `if price > 100 then total = total + price` with no closing keyword  (iii) `pagewidth = priceband * 2` where `priceband` is a text value and `pagewidth` is declared as an integer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage that the compiled form has over the interpreted form for this particular workflow, referring to the number of times the script is run and to what changes between runs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the total time in milliseconds taken by each of the two approaches for a single run, and determine the number of executions at which the two totals become equal. Show your working.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Comment on whether the equality you found in part (c) should decide the choice, referring to what the workflow does between executions.

questions.answer:
**(a)**

(i) `1@5` is **lexical**: the tokeniser's rules define a number as a run of digits and `@` is not a character that can appear in one, so the scanner fails to form a valid token before any grammar is considered (A1). The characters are individually fine; it is the sequence that no token can cover.

(ii) The missing closing keyword is **syntax**. Every token so far is valid -- `if`, an identifier, a relation, a number, the keyword `then`, an assignment -- and it is the arrangement of those tokens that the grammar rejects, because the rule for a conditional requires a terminator (A1). No meaning has been examined yet.

(iii) `priceband * 2` with a text operand is **semantic**. The statement is grammatically well formed and every token is valid; what fails is the check that the types of the operands are compatible with the operator and with the declared type of the target (A1). This check needs the symbol table of declarations, which is why it cannot be done during scanning or parsing.

**(b)** The compiled form pays the translation cost once and then runs cheaply, and on this workflow the script is executed roughly $260$ times a year -- once each weekday -- against a small number of edits. The number of executions is large and the number of *different* versions is small, so the one-off cost is amortised over many runs (M1).

What changes between runs is normally nothing at all: the environmental data comes from the product database, not from the script. The edit that follows a price-band change is the exception, and it does invalidate the translated form; but even if the script were edited once a month, the translation would be repeated twelve times a year against two hundred and sixty executions (A1).

**(c)** One run of the interpreter:
$$12\,000\ \text{tokens} \times 1.5\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

One *first* run of the compiled route:
$$12\,000 \times 60\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1\text{ for the translation}) ,$$
and each subsequent run costs
$$12\,000 \times 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

Let $n$ be the number of executions. The interpreted total is $18n$ milliseconds and the compiled total is $720 + 3n$ milliseconds, both measured from the first run and including it. Setting them equal:
$$18n = 720 + 3n, \qquad 15n = 720, \qquad n = 48 \;\; (A1).$$
After $48$ executions both routes have consumed $864\ \mathrm{ms}$. Under the compiled route the script is executed about $260$ times a year, so the crossover is passed in the tenth week of the first year, and the compiled route is decisively cheaper thereafter: at $260$ executions the interpreted total is $4\,680\ \mathrm{ms}$ against $1\,500\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the compiled one, a saving of about $3.2$ seconds a year.

**(d)** The equality should not decide the choice on its own, because it is derived from a model whose central assumption is that the same script is executed many times unchanged (M1).

The workflow does edit the script: whenever a price band changes, the editor changes the file, and a compiler must then translate the whole thing again at a cost of $720\ \mathrm{ms}$. If the script were edited before every run, the compiled total for $n$ runs would be $n(720 + 3)$ milliseconds against $18n$ for the interpreter, and the compiler would never win. Between the two extremes the answer turns on the edit rate, which the stimulus does not fix. What can be said without that number is that the crossover of $48$ is the edit-free case and therefore the *most favourable* figure the compiler can claim; the real crossover is higher, by $48$ executions for every extra retranslation, and the decision should be taken on a measured edit rate rather than on the model alone (A1).

The model also ignores two things that favour the interpreter: the compiled intermediate form has to be stored and kept in step with its source, which is a real operational cost, and in this workflow the run takes place once a day, so a saving of sixteen milliseconds per run is not visible to anybody. If the only consideration were time, the case for compiling would rest on the tenth week of each year; if the consideration is engineering effort and the risk of a stale translated file, the interpreter may still be the better answer.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for each of the three with a reason. The reason must refer to the stage's own job, not restate the error: "lexical because it is a character that cannot start a token" scores, "lexical because it is a typo" does not. A candidate who places (iii) at syntax has confused a grammar rule with a type rule and scores two of three.

(b) (M1) for using the ratio of executions to distinct versions, (A1) for connecting it to what changes between runs. A candidate who says "compiled code runs faster" without referring to the number of runs scores nothing: the mark is for the amortisation argument, which is the only thing that distinguishes the two approaches here.

(c) (A1) for $18\ \mathrm{ms}$, (A1) for $720\ \mathrm{ms}$ of translation, (A1) for $3\ \mathrm{ms}$ per subsequent run, (A1) for $n = 48$ with the working. A candidate who writes $18n = 720 + 3(n-1)$ obtains $n = 47.8$ and should be given the final mark if they state that $48$ executions is the first at which the compiled total is lower; the difference is whether the first run is counted in both totals, which it should be. A candidate who answers with the per-run ratio ("six times faster") forfeits the last mark; that is exactly the comparison the item is testing.

(d) (M1) for identifying the assumption of an unchanged script, (A1) for a consequence that changes the decision -- a higher crossover, or a crossover that does not exist if the edit rate is high enough. A candidate who says only "the script is edited sometimes" scores the first mark and not the second, because the mark requires the effect of the edit to be traced into the arithmetic.

Condonation: speeds may be quoted in microseconds throughout with the conversion to milliseconds made at the end; the arithmetic is identical. A candidate who states the crossover as "about fifty executions" scores the last mark in (c), provided the exact value is also shown. Forfeits: including the disk read or the process start-up in the totals, which the stem excludes; treating the $12\,000$ tokens as $12\,000$ lines, which changes the arithmetic by a factor the candidate cannot justify.
questions.explanation:
This is an arithmetic question wearing a systems question's clothes, and the arithmetic is not the difficulty. Multiplying a token count by a per-token cost takes a minute; deciding *what to multiply* is the whole of the item.

The instinct, when asked which of two ways of running a program is faster, is to compare the running times: $18\ \mathrm{ms}$ against $3\ \mathrm{ms}$, a ratio of six. That comparison is correct and it is not the answer, because the compiled route has already spent $720\ \mathrm{ms}$ before any of its cheap runs happen. The candid way to put the question is over how many runs the comparison is made, and the answer is a crossover: for any number of runs below $48$, interpreting is cheaper in total. Part (c) asks for that number explicitly, which removes the ambiguity, but part (b) is where the reasoning has to be supplied before the arithmetic can be trusted, because the number of runs is not a property of the language -- it is a property of the workflow.

That is also why part (d) exists. The crossover of $48$ is computed on the assumption that the script never changes, and the stimulus explicitly says that it does change. Each edit forces a retranslation of the whole script, because the cost model given is a whole-script translation and there is no partial translation. So the honest statement is that $48$ is a lower bound on the crossover and the true figure depends on how often the price bands change, which the question deliberately does not supply. Recognising that a model has one unfixed parameter and saying which one it is, is more valuable than producing a confident number that the model does not support.

Part (a) is a separate lesson attached to the same stimulus, and it is the one that turns up in examinations most often. "The compiler finds the errors" is true and useless: the three stages find different errors for different reasons, and the reason is always that stage's own job. A scanner cannot report an undeclared variable because it has no symbol table; a parser cannot report a type mismatch for the same reason; and a semantic analyser never sees a character that could not be tokenised. The three fragments are chosen so that each has exactly one stage that can catch it and two that cannot, and a candidate who has the stages sorted will be able to say which is which without hesitating.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Compiler against interpreter cost comparisons are standard in every A-level and AP-style treatment of translation; the version here fixes the workflow around a daily batch run with occasional hand edits -- the arrangement that makes the one-off translation cost decisive -- and asks for the model's unfixed parameter rather than for a recommendation.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compare the two per-run times by dividing the token count into each per-token cost, find eighteen milliseconds against three, conclude that the compiled form is six times faster, and recommend compiling on the strength of that ratio alone.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The compiled route pays a one-off translation cost of seven hundred and twenty milliseconds before its first cheap run, so the per-run comparison is only valid once that cost has been amortised, and with the stated rates the amortisation takes forty eight executions rather than the one the ratio implies.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The recommendation is to compile, justified by the six-to-one ratio of running times, with no crossover computed and no acknowledgement that the first forty seven executions are more expensive under the compiled route than the interpreted one.

verification.method: Both per-run times were recomputed from the token count and the stated rates, and the crossover was obtained algebraically and then confirmed by evaluating both totals at n = 47, 48 and 49. The annual figures used in the discussion were obtained from 52 weeks x 5 weekdays. The three faulty fragments in part (a) were each checked against a small hand-written tokeniser and grammar for the described language to confirm that only one stage can report each of them.
solution_skeleton: classify each faulty fragment by the stage whose rules it violates
multiply the token count by each per-token rate to obtain the per-run times
add the one-off translation time to the compiled total as a constant term
set the two linear totals equal and solve for the number of executions
examine the model's assumption about how often the source changes between runs

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security, with A4.4 Ethical considerations and A3.2 Database design
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A2.4 A security incident caused by a legitimate account with excessive privilege, where the control that would have prevented it conflicts with the requirement that clinical staff must not be blocked out of records in an emergency
questions.challenge_mechanism: The incident has no attacker and no vulnerability: the account was genuine, the password was correct and the network was up to date. What made the breach possible is that a single technical-support role had been granted every permission that any of its thirty-four holders might ever need, so the requirement that staff are never locked out of a record in an emergency and the requirement that no account holds more privilege than its job needs cannot both be met by one role per person. The quantitative part turns on the number of roles a pure role-based scheme needs and on what that number costs to audit.

stimulus.title: An incident at a three-site hospital trust
stimulus.body:
A hospital trust runs one patient-records system across three sites, with six clinical departments. Access is granted through roles. In the year of the incident the trust operated forty roles; the largest was `TechSupport`, held by thirty-four members of the IT service desk, which carried the union of every permission any of its holders had ever asked for, including read and write access to the full records of every department at every site. The trust's written policy is that no member of staff may be denied access to a record they need in order to treat a patient, and that any access outside a member's own department must be visible in the audit log within one working day.

The incident: a service-desk analyst whose employment was being terminated copied the records of $1{,}180$ patients from four departments he had never worked in and had never had a legitimate reason to view. The copy was made over eleven days using his own account and his own credentials during normal working hours. It was found two months later during a routine audit. Nothing he did required an exploit, a stolen password or a disabled control, and every copy operation was recorded in the log. The log had $4.2$ million entries for the year and was reviewed by one auditor two days a week.

The proposal on the table is to replace the forty roles with a strict role-based scheme in which a role exists for every combination of site, department and job function that the trust employs, and in which any access outside a member's own role is refused by the system and escalated to a manager. The trust employs six departments, five job functions and three sites. The trust's information-governance officer has objected, on the grounds that the strict scheme will create an administration burden the trust cannot carry and that a refused request in a clinical emergency is a patient-safety event.

questions.question: The trust's board has asked for an analysis of the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, a design for a replacement role-based access-control scheme, the working arithmetic of the current audit coverage and the proposed quarterly permission review, and an evaluation of the information-governance officer's objection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, identifying for each component whether it was breached and giving the specific evidence from the case that supports your answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Design a role-based access-control scheme for this trust, stating how many roles the strict scheme described in the case would need and explaining how your design resolves the conflict between the trust's policy on emergency access and the principle of least privilege.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The auditor reviews $4.2$ million log entries a year in two days a week. Determine what fraction of the log is currently reviewed, and determine the review workload the proposed scheme implies if each role must be reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes per role.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the proposal against the information-governance officer's objection, and state which of the two requirements -- least privilege or unblocked clinical access -- your design sacrifices and why.

questions.answer:
**(a)** *Confidentiality* was the component actually breached, and the breach was large and deliberate: $1{,}180$ patients' records were copied by someone who had no legitimate reason to see any of them. The evidence is the volume, the four departments outside his own and the eleven days over which he worked (A1).

*Integrity* was **not** breached on the evidence given. Every operation was a copy out of the system; the case records no modification, deletion or insertion of records, and none of the $1{,}180$ records is stated to have been altered. It is worth saying plainly that the absence of an integrity breach is a fact about this incident and not a property of the design -- the same account carried write access to the full records of every department, so integrity was equally exposed and was simply not attacked (A1).

*Availability* was **not** breached either. The systems remained available to the clinicians who needed them throughout, and nothing in the case suggests service loss. The relevant observation is that the compromise was found two months late, which is a failure of detection rather than of availability; the log contained the evidence from the first day (A1).

The interesting finding is that two of the three components were untouched and the third was breached completely, by a user whose permissions were only what the trust had given him. In a CIA-triple analysis of this incident the useful output is not the tally but the reason each answer comes out as it does.

**(b)** The strict scheme described in the case needs a role for every combination of site, department and job function:
$$3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90 \ \text{roles} \;\; (A1).$$
Against the forty roles in use now, that is a little over twice the number of roles and it is what the governance officer means by an administration burden -- part (c) puts a figure on it.

The design should keep least privilege as the default and treat emergency access as an explicitly-granted, self-expiring exception (M1). Concretely:

1. **Roles are the union of department and job function, not the cross product with site.** A ward nurse is a ward nurse at any of the three sites; the site is an attribute of the *record*, not of the person. That reduces the role count to $6 \times 5 = 30$ and leaves the site as a condition evaluated at request time (A1).
2. **Emergency access is a break-glass grant, not a role.** A clinician who needs a record outside their role requests it, states a reason code, and is given time-limited access -- an hour is long enough for a clinical decision -- with notification to the responsible manager and an entry in the log that is machine-flagged. The clinical requirement is met in seconds, and the exception is narrow, time-bound and attributable (A1).
3. **The audit becomes targeted.** What matters for detection is the small set of accesses outside a member's usual pattern, not the $4.2$ million entries. Flagging break-glass grants, out-of-own-department reads and reads at volume per user per day reduces the reviewer's queue to something a human can actually read (A1).

**(c)** The auditor works two days a week, which is $2 \times 52 = 104$ working days a year, or about $\dfrac{104}{5} = 20.8$ working weeks (M1). Reviewing $4.2$ million entries at, say, one entry per second would take
$$\frac{4{,}200{,}000}{3600 \times 7} = 166.7 \ \text{seven-hour days},$$
against the $104$ days available; so even at one entry per second the log cannot be read in the time the trust gives it, and the true coverage is a small fraction of a per cent (A1). The practical statement is that the log as configured is not a control at all: it is a record that exists so that a breach can be reconstructed afterwards, which is exactly how this incident was found.

The proposed scheme's review workload is a different quantity and it is small by comparison. Ninety roles reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes each:
$$90 \times 15 = 1{,}350 \ \text{minutes} = 22.5 \ \text{hours per quarter},$$
or $7.5$ hours a month (A1). Under the reduced design of part (b), with thirty roles, the same review costs $30 \times 15 = 450$ minutes $= 7.5$ hours per quarter, a third of the strict scheme's burden. Note the direction of the comparison: the *permission review* is affordable under either scheme and the *log review* is not affordable under either, so the governance officer's objection is about the wrong quantity.

**(d)** The objection is half right. The administration burden of ninety roles is real but small in absolute terms -- $22.5$ hours a quarter is a fraction of one person's time -- and it is not the reason the strict scheme should be rejected. The patient-safety objection is the serious one, because a system that refuses a clinician access to a record in an emergency has converted a security control into a clinical hazard, and no audit finding justifies that (A1).

My design sacrifices something, and it is least privilege in the strict sense: a break-glass grant means that for a short period a member of staff holds access their role does not include. What is preserved is the part of least privilege that matters -- that the excess access is bounded in time, requires a stated reason, is attributable to a person and is reported rather than discovered (A1). The alternative, refusing the request, protects the principle absolutely and harms patients; the alternative of granting standing access to everyone who might ever need it, which is what the trust actually did, is what produced this incident. Sacrificing a strict reading of the principle in favour of an auditable exception is the trade the case is designed to force, and the mark is for saying which side of it the design comes down on and why.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for each component with evidence. The marks are for the *evidence*, not the verdict: "confidentiality breached because 1,180 records were copied by someone with no reason to see them" scores, "confidentiality was breached" does not. A candidate who claims integrity or availability was breached must point to a modification or an outage in the case; the case contains neither and claiming one forfeits that component's mark.

(b) (A1) for $3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90$, (M1) for a design that separates the two requirements rather than trading one away, (A1) for the site-as-attribute reduction, (A1) for the break-glass mechanism with its time limit, reason code and notification, (A1) for the targeted audit. Full marks do not require all four design elements; a candidate who gives the role count, the site attribute and the break-glass mechanism has the substance. A design that answers "give everyone less access" without saying what happens in an emergency scores (A1) and (M1) only.

(c) (M1) for converting the auditor's time into days or weeks, (A1) for the conclusion that the log cannot be read at any realistic rate, (A1) for $22.5$ hours per quarter from the ninety roles. A candidate who computes $90 \times 15$ and stops has the third mark; the first two require the comparison. Accept $104$ days, $20.8$ weeks or a "small fraction of a per cent" as the statement of coverage.

(d) (A1) for separating the two objections and treating the clinical one as the serious one, (A1) for naming what the design gives up, (A1) for tracing a consequence of that choice -- what bounds the relaxation (its lifetime, its reason code, its reportability) or what fails clinically if the request is refused instead. A candidate who says "both requirements can be satisfied" without saying which is relaxed in the emergency case scores at most the first mark.

Forfeits: describing the incident as an external attack, which the case explicitly denies; proposing encryption as the primary control, which does nothing about an authorised user; proposing to remove the technical-support account, which leaves the support function unable to work. Condonation: role counts of $30$ or $90$ are both accepted in (b) provided the scheme described matches the number given.
questions.explanation:
The most useful thing about this case is what it does not contain. There is no attacker, no exploit, no stolen credential and no unpatched system. A member of staff with a valid account read records he was allowed to read. Every control that a checklist would name as present *was* present, which is why the case is worth studying: the failure is in the permission model, and the permission model was somebody's deliberate answer to a real operational problem.

The problem it answered is stated in the case and it is usually stated in real hospitals too: staff must never be blocked from a record they need in order to treat a patient. The cheapest way to guarantee that is to give a support role every permission any of its thirty-four holders might need, because then no request is ever refused. The cost of that answer is invisible until it is not: one analysis of the log would have shown that a service-desk analyst was reading four departments he had never worked in, eleven days running, and the log had the evidence from the first day. Detection failed because there was nothing small enough to look at -- $4.2$ million entries, one auditor, two days a week -- and the arithmetic in part (c) is there to make that failure a number rather than an opinion.

The design question is therefore not "how do we stop insiders" but "how do we keep the guarantee without the blanket permission", and the answer that works is to make the exception explicit and short-lived. Break-glass access is a genuine technique and its properties are exactly the ones the case needs: the clinician gets the record in seconds, the grant expires on its own, the reason is recorded, and the manager is notified. Least privilege in the strict sense -- nobody holds any permission they do not need -- is given up for the duration of the grant, and part (d) asks the candidate to say so out loud rather than pretend the trade does not exist.

The role arithmetic is deliberately unremarkable. Three sites times six departments times five functions is ninety, and a candidate who sees that the site belongs to the record rather than to the person gets it down to thirty. Neither number is frightening on its own -- twenty-two hours a quarter is not a burden -- and the point of computing both is to show that the governance officer has objected to the wrong quantity. The scheme that the trust actually ran had forty roles and still produced this incident, which is the clearest evidence that counting roles is not the control.

provenance.adaptation: Original. Insider misuse of legitimately-granted privilege and the break-glass pattern are both well documented in health-informatics practice; the case here is written to put them in conflict on purpose, and adds the working arithmetic of a log that cannot be read so that the detection failure is quantified rather than asserted.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Treat the incident as a permissions problem and tighten the roles, either by cutting the technical-support role down to its documented duties or by building a role for every combination of site, department and job function so that nobody holds anything they do not need.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Both tightenings collide with the trust's other written policy, which guarantees that no member of staff is denied a record needed to treat a patient, so a scheme that refuses access outside a role converts a security control into a clinical hazard and cannot be shipped unchanged.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The recommendation is a strict role-based scheme with a role per site, department and function, justified by least privilege, with the emergency-access policy treated as an operational matter to be handled by a manager override that the design never specifies.

verification.method: The role count was computed as the product of the three stated dimensions and compared with the forty roles in use. The audit arithmetic was computed twice, once as the number of seven-hour days needed at one log entry per second and once as the fraction of the auditor's available days, and both were checked against the totals stated in the case. The permission-review workload was computed for both the ninety-role and the thirty-role design.
solution_skeleton: test each component of the confidentiality integrity availability triple against the case evidence
multiply the three dimensions of the access matrix to count the roles a strict scheme requires
separate the standing permission from the emergency exception and give the exception a lifetime
convert the auditor's available time and the log volume into comparable units
state which requirement the chosen design relaxes and what bounds the relaxation

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only), with B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class and B2.2 Data structures
questions.topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
questions.subtopic: B3.2 Two independent classification axes modelled with inheritance, where the obvious hierarchy multiplies out and the correct design uses composition to keep the two axes separate
questions.challenge_mechanism: The naive hierarchy is not wrong, it is merely multiplicative: with four formats and five genres, a class per combination gives twenty subclasses, and adding one format costs five more. The design that keeps the axes separate gives nine classes and adding a format costs one. The judgement the item asks for is *when* the multiplicative hierarchy is nevertheless the right answer, and there is a real answer to that, which the last part requires.

stimulus.title: A media catalogue for a school library
stimulus.body:
A library system stores entries for its collection. Each entry has a **format**, which is one of four: `Print`, `Audio`, `Video` or `Download`. Each entry also has a **genre**, which is one of five: `Fiction`, `Reference`, `Biography`, `Poetry` or `Periodical`. Format and genre vary independently: the library holds every combination except `Download` with `Periodical`, which it has decided never to stock, so there are nineteen combinations in use out of a possible twenty. Every entry also has a title, an author or creator, a shelf location and a loan period.

Behaviour depends on both axes. A format dictates how a copy is lent (a print copy can be recalled, a download expires, an audio copy has a play count), and a genre dictates how the entry is catalogued and which subject headings apply. A later release will add a fifth format, `Microform`, and a sixth genre, `Drama`.

A junior developer has proposed a class hierarchy with one abstract class `MediaEntry` and a concrete subclass for each combination: `PrintFiction`, `PrintReference`, `PrintBiography`, and so on.

questions.question: The library must decide whether to accept the junior developer's hierarchy. Identify the two axes of classification and the data and operations that belong to each, explain how many concrete classes the proposal contains in use and in full, design an alternative structure that keeps the axes separate, and justify a situation in which the multiplicative hierarchy would nevertheless be the better choice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two axes of classification in this system and, for each, state one piece of data and one operation that depends on it rather than on the other axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how many concrete classes the proposed hierarchy contains in use and how many it would contain if it covered every possible combination including the one the library has decided never to stock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Design an alternative class structure that keeps the two axes separate, state how many classes it contains, and state what it costs to add the proposed fifth format.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Justify a situation in which the junior developer's multiplicative hierarchy would be the better choice despite the larger class count.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The two axes are **format** ('Print', 'Audio', 'Video', 'Download') and **genre** ('Fiction', 'Reference', 'Biography', 'Poetry', 'Periodical') (A1).

A datum that depends on format rather than on genre: the media type stored with a copy, or a play count or an expiry date -- all of these are properties of how the thing is carried, and none of them changes when a biography is reclassified as reference (A1). An operation that depends on format: `renew()`, which behaves differently for a print copy that can be recalled and a download that expires. A datum that depends on genre: the list of subject headings, or the Dewey-class code. An operation that depends on genre: `catalogue()`, or `suggestSimilar()`, which works on subject matter and is indifferent to whether the item is a download or a video (A1).

The test in each case is whether a change on the *other* axis would force a change here. Reclassifying a novel as poetry changes the subject headings and changes nothing about how it is lent; converting the same title from print to audio changes how it is lent and changes nothing about its subject headings.

**(b)** In use the library holds every combination except 'Download' with 'Periodical', so the proposal needs
$$4 \times 5 - 1 = 19 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1).$$
It also needs at least one method to differ between them, or the subclasses are empty shells that exist only to carry a name.

Covering every combination gives
$$4 \times 5 = 20 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1),$$
one more than the number in use. The difference is worth noticing in the other direction: the proposal is already nineteen classes and the library intends to add a fifth format and a sixth genre, which takes the in-use count from nineteen to
$$5 \times 6 - 1 = 29,$$
an addition of ten classes for two changes to the specification.

**(c)** A design that keeps the axes apart uses two small hierarchies and lets each entry hold one of each:

- a `Format` hierarchy with an abstract `Format` and four subclasses (`Print`, `Audio`, `Video`, `Download`), each implementing `lend()` and `renew()` (A1);
- a `Genre` hierarchy with an abstract `Genre` and five subclasses (`Fiction`, `Reference`, `Biography`, `Poetry`, `Periodical`), each implementing `headings()` (A1);
- a single `MediaEntry` class holding a title, a creator, a location, a loan period, one `Format` object and one `Genre` object, and delegating the format-specific and genre-specific operations to whichever objects it holds (A1).

The class count is $2$ abstract bases $+\ 4$ formats $+\ 5$ genres $+\ 1$ entry $= 12$ classes in total, of which the two abstract bases carry no instances and the concrete working classes number ten. The library's existing nineteen combinations are expressed as nineteen *objects* of `MediaEntry`, not as nineteen classes.

Adding `Microform` means writing one new subclass of `Format` and changing nothing else: the count of classes goes up by one, no `MediaEntry` code changes, and the combination of `Microform` with each of the five genres works immediately. Under the proposal the same change would add five classes, each of which would need its own `lend()` and `renew()` implementations even though they would be identical.

**(d)** The multiplicative hierarchy is the better choice when the two axes do not merely coexist but **interact**, that is when the behaviour of a combination is not the sum of what the two axes would do separately (A1).

A concrete case from this system: a `DownloadPeriodical` may be barred from the collection, and a `PrintPeriodical` must be lent with a shorter period than other print material. If a rule of that kind applies to one cell of the grid and to no other, then the cell has behaviour of its own, and the cleanest place for it is a subclass that exists to hold it. Composition would express the same thing with a conditional inside `MediaEntry`, and a conditional that tests the pair of axes is exactly a hard-coded combination in a different place (A1).

The general statement is worth giving: composition is preferred when the axes can be combined freely and their behaviour composes; inheritance is preferred when the combinations have their own behaviour. Here nineteen of the twenty cells behave as the composition of their row and column, so composition is right, and a candidate who says so and identifies the one cell that would justify the other design has understood the distinction rather than the rule of thumb.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for naming both axes, (A1) for a format-dependent datum or operation, (A1) for a genre-dependent one. The two examples must be *different in kind* or the mark is not awarded twice for the same idea: a candidate who gives `playCount` for format and `shelfLocation` for genre scores the first two marks only if the shelf location is shown to be genre-independent, which it is not -- location is a property of neither axis and is a generic attribute. A candidate who gives `headings()` for genre and `lend()` for format scores all three.

(b) (A1) for nineteen, (A1) for twenty, with the reason for the difference stated or implied. A candidate who writes twenty twice has not read the exception and scores one mark.

(c) (A1) for the format hierarchy, (A1) for the genre hierarchy, (A1) for a single entry class that holds one of each. The class count is not itself marked in this part, but a candidate who produces two hierarchies and no entry class has not designed a structure that can hold the nineteen combinations and cannot score the third mark. Counting the classes as ten, twelve or "nine concrete plus one entry" is all accepted provided the arithmetic matches the structure described.

(d) (A1) for the general criterion -- the axes interact, or some cells have behaviour of their own -- (A1) for a specific example from this system. "When the combinations are genuinely different" without an example scores the first mark only.

Condonation: a candidate who uses an interface rather than an abstract class scores the same; so does one who makes `Format` and `Genre` enumerations with a strategy object per value, provided the two axes remain separate. Forfeits: proposing a single class with a `format` field and a `genre` field and a long `if`-`else` chain over both, which does express the two axes but puts all the behaviour in one class -- a candidate who explains that the behaviour is still separated by dispatching on the held objects scores full credit, and one who simply nests the conditionals does not.
questions.explanation:
The distinction this item is built on is old and it is still got wrong constantly: inheritance models *what something is*, and composition models *what something has*. The library entry is a print copy and it is a work of fiction, and both statements are true, and neither of them is more fundamental than the other. When a designer picks one of the two axes and hangs inheritance off it, they have quietly decided that the other axis will be handled by something else -- and if there is no plan for that, the other axis gets handled by a class per combination.

That is how the nineteen subclasses appear. Nobody chooses twenty classes for a two-dimensional problem; it happens because the first axis is modelled properly with four subclasses, and then the second axis has nowhere to live, and the path of least resistance is a subclass. The tell is that the subclasses come in groups of five or four with identical bodies, differing only in their name.

Composition removes the multiplication because the two axes become two *objects* held by one class, and objects compose where classes multiply. The entry delegates `lend()` to its format object and `headings()` to its genre object, and the number of classes stops depending on the product of the two list lengths. The numbers are small enough here to check by hand: nineteen against twelve, and the addition of a format costs one class against five. That comparison is the argument, and it is why the item asks for the counts rather than for a design principle.

Part (d) is where a candidate who has only memorised "prefer composition" is separated from one who has understood it. There is a real case for the multiplicative hierarchy, and it is not a rare one: when a specific cell of the grid has behaviour that neither axis explains, the cell is an entity and deserves a class. A download periodical that is barred from the collection is such a cell. The point is not that composition is always right; it is that composition is right when the grid's behaviour composes, and a designer who knows which of the two situations they are in has the whole of the answer.

provenance.adaptation: Adapted from the standard A-level treatment of class design for multiple classes, which usually presents inheritance as the solution. The rewrite keeps the two-axis catalogue but arranges the specification so that the axes are independent, which makes inheritance multiplicative rather than merely bulky, and adds a final part that requires the candidate to say when the multiplicative design is nevertheless correct.
provenance.resource_origin: A-level Computer Science object-oriented design with inheritance and composition

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Model the catalogue with inheritance as the specification's two lists suggest, creating an abstract entry class and a subclass for each combination of format and genre, because each named format and each named genre looks like something the system is and therefore something the type system should represent.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The two axes vary independently, so an inheritance tree over one of them leaves the other with nowhere to live and the classes multiply, and the correct structure is composition in which one entry object holds one format object and one genre object so that a change to one list adds one class rather than one class per member of the other list.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The design reported is an abstract base with nineteen concrete subclasses, and the extensibility question is answered by agreeing that adding a format will require five or six new subclasses, which is treated as a normal cost of the design rather than as the symptom of it.

verification.method: The class counts were computed as products over the stated dimensions for both designs and checked against the specification's exception for the download periodical. The cost of adding a format was computed for each design as the number of new classes required. The example used in the justification was checked against the stimulus to confirm that it is a rule about one cell of the grid rather than a rule about a row.
solution_skeleton: separate the two classification axes and test which behaviour belongs to which
multiply the axis lengths to count the classes the multiplicative design requires
model each axis as its own small hierarchy and let one entry hold one of each
count the classes in the separated design and the classes one new format adds
identify the condition under which a single cell of the grid has behaviour of its own
